In that case, being non-deceptive refers to the absence of contradiction; this is the authentic state. Why is this so? Because in a dream, one may perceive the same thing again or even something else. The phrase "this is" refers to the enjoyment of great joy. The phrase "due to awareness" means that at that very moment, one experiences the performance of a function, and is thus non-deceptive. Therefore, the meaning is that both waking and dreaming states are considered valid cognition or its opposite based on whether they are non-deceptive or otherwise.

If one thinks: "Since dream and waking are distinguished as being false or otherwise simply by being seen as such, why is any other cause for differentiation needed?" The text says "dream and the other." Mere individual appearance does not differentiate between the two, because there is no distinction <note>in the quality of appearance itself</note>. The meaning is that the distinction between being deceptive and otherwise has not been established.

Is it not unreasonable to say "because there is no focal object <term>alambana</term> for this" regarding the pleasure grove? Because saying "it does not exist" is not a focal object, for the thought "it does not exist" is itself the focal object. If one thinks: "If it is free from dependence and is known, will it not fail to arise even slightly?" The text says, "the knowledge that this does not exist." The phrase "realized by another" refers to <note>realization</note> through direct perception or inference.

Form, taste, and so forth are realized by the direct perception in which they appear. Therefore, existence itself is not apparent because it is secluded and free from other things. Because it is of the very nature of being secluded from that, it is known; even if it is not known by the appropriate subjects, it is known by itself. The knowledge that follows only the nature of being free from that is the mental determination that acts as the producer of its own form. Therefore, to show that the focal object of this is nothing other than mental determination, the text says "becoming like that." Even that which arises from habitual tendencies <term>vasana</term> is its distinction.

<summary>This page discusses the criteria for non-deceptive cognition in waking and dreaming states, arguing that the distinction lies in functional consistency rather than the mere appearance of objects. It explores the nature of mental determination and how the absence of an object can itself serve as a focal point for awareness.</summary>
<keywords>non-deceptive, valid cognition, dreaming, waking, focal object, mental determination, habitual tendencies, vasana, alambana</keywords>

Therefore, when it is said that it is pervaded by one part of the property belonging to the subject to be proven <note>the <term>dharmin</term></note>, it will be understood that it is pervaded by the property to be proven <note>the <term>sadhya-dharma</term></note>. If one asks, "Is the subject itself not also one part of that?", it is true, but it is impossible for it to be pervaded by that, because it is the nature of the qualifier <note>original: "viśeṣa"</note>. If it is argued that pervasion is not perceived in the qualifier but is not actually nonexistent, this is incorrect. This is because pervasion is the nature of positive and negative concomitance <note>original: "anvaya-vyatireka"</note>, and because those exist everywhere as their nature, and also because a qualifier is impossible there. Therefore, the meaning that the property of the subject to be proven is pervaded by the property to be proven is the reason <note>original: "hetu"</note> will be understood.

Having explained "by a part of the property of the subject," the term "pervasion" <note>original: "vyāpti"</note> is mentioned in order to explain its nature. It is called pervasion because the pervader <note>original: "vyāpaka"</note> encompasses the pervaded <note>original: "vyāpya"</note>. To state this is to express the specific, individually determined nature of those two. Therefore, the specific nature of the pervader is expressed exactly as it is; there is no separate "action" <note>original: "kriyā"</note> at all. Here, regarding the three words, the determination <note>original: "avadhāraṇa"</note> can occur in three ways: "only that," "only the qualifier," and "only existence." 

In this context, since it is appropriate that the understanding of the qualifier leads to the understanding of the pervader, it is shown that "pervasion by its part is the reason." This is shown because the positive and negative concomitance of the pervaded exists in the qualifier itself, and because those very things function as the proof in making the reason understood. Therefore, when the proof exists, the existence of the thing to be proven is individually determined; thus, when expressing the nature that makes it understood as a reason, it should be said that "only the pervader exists." In that case, if one determines that "only the pervader exists," the property that makes it understood will not be shown, because the pervaded stands near—

<summary>This page explains the logical relationship between the subject, the property to be proven, and the nature of pervasion in Buddhist logic. It clarifies that the logical reason must be pervaded by the property to be proven through the mechanism of positive and negative concomitance.</summary>
<keywords>pervasion, vyapti, subject, dharmin, property, dharma, reason, hetu, qualifier, visesha, concomitance, anvaya-vyatireka</keywords>

One must state why it is not solitary <note>original: "འབའ་ཞིག་མ་ཡིན་པ"</note>. The proponent of the philosophical tenet states: "Because it is momentary." The specific nature <note>original: "རང་གི་ངོ་བོ་"</note> of this <note>the cause</note> which is concurrent with and joined with its cooperative conditions is precisely that which has been the first moment of its own nature since beginningless <term>samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of existence</gloss>. Therefore, its nature is established as being momentary. How then could it be solitary?

If one thinks that it must also be proven that a single momentary thing produces an effect that arises in that moment, for that reason it is said: "How it is produced has already been explained." How an effect is produced while remaining in a single moment has already been explained in the preceding section where it was said: "Since they neither existed before nor will exist after, and they are not of a distinct nature either." When that is the case, how could a thing possessing the capacity to produce an effect without interruption in a single moment exist before, after, or as something distinct? Because this possesses the character of arising from only a single moment, it is "that which arises in a single moment."

In some manuscripts <note>original: "གླེགས་བམ་ལ་ལ་ལས་"</note> it appears as "arising at that moment." This means that because it has the character of arising only at that very moment which is intended here, the phrase should be construed as "arising at that moment." The terms "before," "after," and "separately" are explained here as terms for "becoming otherwise." 

If one thinks: "We see only that seeds and such which have not formed a collection <note>original: "ཚོགས་པར་མ་གྱུར་པ་"</note> exist before, and then after being separated from the collection, they exist separately and subsequently as something that has become otherwise," for that reason it is said: "That which becomes otherwise," and so forth. That which has not formed a collection and that which is separated and made distinct from a collection is not the very same entity that has the nature of producing an effect without delay. Therefore, concerning the statement that results in the absurdity: "Why does a momentary thing not produce an effect solitarily, or why is it not solitary?" 

<summary>This page discusses the Buddhist logic of momentariness, arguing that causes produce effects through a collection of conditions in a single moment rather than as solitary, enduring entities. It refutes the idea that a cause can remain the same while its capacity to produce an effect changes over time.</summary>
<keywords>momentariness, causation, cooperative conditions, philosophical tenets, Buddhist logic, samsara, collection of conditions</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>exclusion <note>Sanskrit: apoha; the exclusion of other possibilities</note> should not be accepted as the meaning of words. If you ask, "Why is it negated?" the response is, "That is not a deceiver" <note>original: "na sa lu byed min"</note>. By "that," he refers to words and such which are not exclusions. The term "is a deceiver" <note>original: "slu byed yin"</note> means that which does not act without deception, or it is a deceiver because it lacks non-deception.

If you ask why, it is because it lacks a connection to real entities. Such things lack a connection to functional entities, and as established previously, the meaning of words characterized as universals <note>Sanskrit: jāti</note> and so forth has been refuted as being a real entity. Well then, if that is the case, if the meaning of a word as exclusion is refuted in favor of words that are not exclusions, how can any understanding arise? To this he says, "All cognitions arising from words..." <note>original: "sgra las byུང་ ba'i shes pa kun"</note>. Some cognitions arising from words arise as a false attachment to unreal objects simply through the power of habitual tendencies <note>Sanskrit: vāsanā</note> involving incorrect conceptualization. Consequently, it is not the case that things exist or do not exist by the power of such cognitions.

Regarding the statement, "Of the words such as 'knowable' <note>Sanskrit: jñeya</note>..." and so forth, he mentions the word "knowable" and others. Regarding whom does one say, "There is nothing to be excluded by the word 'knowable' and so forth"? For a moment, if one relies on the word "knowable" in isolation, not residing in a sentence and devoid of connection to other words, then to state it would be to prove what is already proven. This is because there is no purpose, as there is no application of an isolated word. To demonstrate this, he says, "By the wise, suddenly..." In this context, "isolated" refers to being unconnected to other words. "Suddenly" means outside of the particular context. Because wise persons apply words for the sake of assisting the listener, not out of mere attachment. By applying an isolated word, a listener is not assisted by the character of reversing doubt and misconception. Thus, if a teacher acts to reverse the doubt and misconception that have arisen in a listener regarding an isolated term and to produce a cognition free of doubt, then he would be assisting that person. Otherwise...

<summary>This page discusses the linguistic theory of exclusion (apoha), arguing that words lack a direct connection to real entities and that isolated terms fail to provide the communicative assistance necessary to resolve a listener's doubts.</summary>
<keywords>exclusion, apoha, linguistics, cognition, habitual tendencies, vāsanā, knowable, jñeya, semantics</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: Although it is said that something</meta> non-existent in essence would also be subject to birth and death, like a person desired <note>mental image or hallucination</note>, this is not the case because there is no distinction <note>between various types of non-existence</note>. If that were so, then delusion without a seed <note>an underlying cause or predisposition</note>, even if appearing as an inversion <note>distorted reality</note>, would not occur. That <note>absolute reality</note> is not of the same class as this <note>deluded appearance</note>. By whom is it seen? By all those who are not <term>paramadarśana</term> <gloss>seers of the ultimate</gloss>. This refers to those other than the Buddhas, whose state is corrupted by the duality of subject and object. Only a Buddha knows suchness <note>the way things truly are</note>; others do not. Although the Buddha, the Blessed One, has fully distinguished the nature of the inverted <note>distorted appearance</note>, he established it in accordance with how it is seen <note>by ordinary beings</note>. Thus, the cause for attachment is shown.

If suchness is not logical for those who are not seers of the ultimate, why mention "the grasped" and so forth? Because those who are not seers of the ultimate are never without the corruption of the grasped <note>object</note> and the grasper <note>subject</note>. Because they are constantly corrupted by the aspects of grasping and being grasped, such seeing and such corruption are neither ultimate nor noble. Since they lack the vision of the ultimate, which is devoid of these two <note>subject and object</note>, how could they know suchness? This is because they have not uprooted the <term>vasana</term> <gloss>habitual tendencies</gloss> of duality. When they see the absence of these two, they will see suchness, for suchness is characterized by being devoid of these two.

For that reason, regarding that very meaning which is characterized by equanimity—meaning the suchness that is free from defined characteristics and remains in equanimity—the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, adopt the "gaze of the elephant" <note>a steady, direct, and all-encompassing look</note>. Just as an elephant looks, though they have seen the suchness of reality, they act as if they do not see it themselves <note>from their own ultimate perspective</note>. 

->With a heart focused solely on the world,<-
->They engage in worldly conduct.<-

Having acted for the sake of those who are attached to the meaning of how the world appears, they say: "Understand it exactly as it appears! Do not cling to what is contrary to how it appears!" Thus they establish the characteristics of external and internal entities.

<summary>This page discusses the distinction between the deluded perception of ordinary beings and the enlightened vision of the Buddha, explaining that while Buddhas see the ultimate suchness devoid of subject-object duality, they teach using the conventional appearances of the world to guide others.</summary>
<keywords>suchness, duality, subject and object, Buddha, elephant gaze, equanimity, habitual tendencies, conventional truth, ultimate truth</keywords>

Nor is it a fourth kind either.
For example, when there are three sons,
because one of those sons is beloved,
the world says "he is the only son."
In the same way, this should be viewed here too.
Because of the connection where one does not occur without the presence of the other,
it never exists in the three modes <note>referring to the *trairūpya* or three conditions of a valid reason: presence in the subject, presence in the similar class, and absence in the dissimilar class</note>.
In the aspect where it is otherwise impossible,
one is observed to exist in the logical reason.
Whatever is "impossibility otherwise" <note>original: *anyathānupapatti*; the principle that the reason cannot exist without the thing to be proven</note>
is itself the logical reason;
whether the two examples exist or not,
they are not its cause.
Wherever there is "impossibility otherwise,"
what need is there for the three <note>the three modes/conditions</note>?
"He is dark-complexioned because he is that father's son,
just like the appearance of the other <note>son</note>."
Even if there are three modes in this case,
it does not function for the sake of certainty.
Aside from those two examples,
it is a logical reason of a single characteristic.
Whether it is an entity or a non-entity, having the nature of existence,
it is because it is perceived in any way whatsoever.
Because one says "the one having a rabbit" <note>an epithet for the moon</note>,
it is not the case that the one marked by a rabbit is not the moon.
This is the second characteristic.
Other logical reasons should also be stated:
From the perception arising from the touch
of a gadfly landing,
one knows with certainty: "This sensation
was caused by being with a gadfly."
In the activity of perceiving form,
the eye is fully endowed with capacity,
because of performing an activity toward that,
and also because of seeing it.
Furthermore, the self, the pot, and so forth,
howsoever they are of the nature of non-existence,
is because they are not perceived in any way whatsoever,
just like <note>referring to the previous line</note> a horn connected to a donkey.
Even the horns of a rabbit and the like,
howsoever they have the nature of existence,
is because they are perceived in any way whatsoever,
as for example the self and the son and so forth.
"Your father is also in this house,"
is something to be known,
because the very sound of your father
is heard in this house.
Regarding entities such as sound and lamps,
there is the "impossibility otherwise."
Even if the property of the subject <note>original: *pakṣadharma*</note> does not exist as an entity,
it is seen to function as a means of realization.
Therefore, the logical reason of a single characteristic
is the primary means of realization.
What use have you for analyzing other things,
such as the property of the subject, which are pointless?
That logical reason endowed with this characteristic:
is it to be realized through a general <note>universal</note> term?
Or is it desired to be known...

<summary>The text argues for the principle of "impossibility otherwise" (anyathānupapatti) as the essential characteristic of a logical reason, suggesting that the traditional three modes of logic are often redundant or merely conventional.</summary>
<keywords>logic, anyathānupapatti, trairūpya, inference, logical reason, epistemology, perception</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>that being's existence is already shown to be that very nature itself. Well then, how is it that a fire which does not produce smoke is still fire itself? Or how is it that smoke produced by smoke becomes smoke itself? There is no fault here, for we have accepted that specific distinction between fire and smoke, rather than merely fire in general. We negate that which is not fire as being the cause, but we do not claim that all fire is the cause <note>specifically of smoke</note>. Or rather, it is not so; since fire is not separate from the suitability to produce smoke, it has already been shown elsewhere that from its very arising, its nature of providing benefit does not fluctuate.

If there also exists fire that does not produce smoke, is it not the case that fire in general is not the producer of smoke? If so, this would be a specific differentiation, just like momentariness and so on; therefore, even if it were separated from fire-ness itself, would it become a different species? Or else, should it be said that smoke is not in error regarding fire as its cause in some other way?

It is said: Even if fire itself possesses distinctions, there certainly exist distinctions that have become its own essence. If it were not so, then because fire itself would be undifferentiated while the distinctions were different, one would be forced to accept a universal <note>original: <term>samanya</term> <gloss>general category or universal</gloss></note>. Therefore, just as there is differentiation by fire-ness itself, so too is it the case with those that produce smoke and those that do not produce smoke; thus there is no fault at all.

When the head of Indra <note>original: <term>Indra</term> <gloss>the king of gods; here referring to a specific plant or substance named after him</gloss></note> is of a nature that is not fire, if smoke were to arise from that head of Indra which is not a cause of smoke, then that <note>non-fire</note> would become the cause, fire. If it does not arise from what is dissimilar, and because a difference in cause produces a difference <note>in effect</note>, and because the production of smoke is the very form of fire, smoke does not arise from what is not fire. Thus, if one speaks without error regarding fire, how could smoke arise from a different, dissimilar co-operating cause or from what is not fire?

Regarding that, it is said: "Now, from different co-operating causes..." and so forth. Those are dissimilar by their very difference and are of a nature that is not fire. By the manner already explained, the effect...

<summary>This page discusses the causal relationship between fire and smoke, arguing that the capacity to produce smoke is inherent to the nature of fire, even if not all fires are actively producing smoke at all times.</summary>
<keywords>causality, fire and smoke, nature, essence, Indra's head, universal, difference</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>the nature of the [object] cannot be determined as its very object. This conceptualization arises from the latent tendencies produced by the cognition of existence, non-existence, and both. Due to the influence of adhering to the appearances within it, it is described as having the qualities of an entity, a non-entity, or both. Therefore, regarding that subject, one contemplates whether this appearing object, which arises from words like <term>Pradhana</term> <gloss>Primordial Matter/Nature</gloss>, is fundamentally based on a functional entity or not, and whether it exists or does not exist.

In establishing that it is not based on a functional entity, that object which should not be rejected because it is personally experienced is the subject. It cannot be said that this object is a <term>svalaksana</term> <gloss>specifically characterized reality/self-character</gloss> because it does not cease to be perceived even regarding objects that have not been obtained or have already ceased, and because it appears even in the cognitions of other non-Buddhist sectarians who possess a distorted adherence to functional entities.

If it were to exclusively engage with the ultimate reality,
Then for the various other systems of tenets,
Words would not engage with their objects
Without a cause;
And even regarding the past and the unborn,
Certain words would not have
Objects that are false;
Therefore, these are held to be the objects of the mind’s focus.

These are the summary verses. Regarding the claim that [the subject] is not based on a functional entity as desired, since there is the quality of such a thing not being observed, the proving quality is not unestablished. Here, it is not even the case that one is referring to the very object appearing in the verbal conceptualization, because words are applied for the sake of establishing that in the mind, and because if that [object] were absent, the [word] would be improper. Furthermore:

By those who do not deny the object of words,
Entities themselves should be examined
By the distinctions of existing and non-existing sides,
Because the arising of results depends on that.

Whether the object of a word exists or does not exist, the purpose of a person is not slightly impaired or accomplished by it, because it is not the suchness <note>reality as it is</note> that corresponds to how one adheres to it; and because that suchness...

<summary>This page argues that the objects of words and conceptual thought are not external functional entities but are mental constructs shaped by latent tendencies. It uses a summary verse to explain why language can refer to non-existent or past things without being grounded in ultimate reality.</summary>
<keywords>conceptualization, latent tendencies, Pradhana, specifically characterized reality, svalaksana, logic, non-existence, mental objects</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta> consciousness itself is taught as the example. Therefore, the phrase "that is why" concludes the refutation of the support <note>the physical basis or substrate</note>. What is the use of speaking at length? For a moment, consider whatever is a functional thing that perishes; it either depends on something else or it does not. In the first case, there is no purpose for a cause that makes that thing remain, because a perishing agent does not remain precisely because it remains as itself. In the second case as well, there is no capacity. The term "plurality" <note>original: "rnams"</note> is a plural word used because of the desire to express the distinct manifestations. If the support makes a state of perishing from itself or from another, then at that time, everything that possesses birth also possesses a remaining support. The rest is easy to understand. Furthermore, the object to be maintained either perishes itself or it does not perish. Here too, respectively, there is either incapacity or lack of necessity. Previously, by analyzing the very position of perishing accepted by others, the two faults were averted; this is the distinction. Regarding the summary, he wishes to speak with a remainder. This means these are the verses that summarize what was expressed and what was implied by the meaning. 

In the ultimate sense, that which dwells in the object does not even meet with the object. Why is that? He says, "by the mind." That belongs to the object. The intention is that the mental consciousness itself, which performs the linking <note>the connection between moments or objects</note>, is the "being" <term>sattva</term> <gloss>sentient being/heroic mind</gloss>. If it is argued that even in non-conceptual states, there is nothing other than the mere aspect of meeting the object, that is true. In non-conceptual states, the designation of "meeting" is concordant, because there is an experience of a clear aspect toward that object. In conceptual thought, it is not like that, because it follows after the parts of the object and the aspect. For that very reason, he says "in the ultimate sense." 

The lamp has a nature characterized by waning and increasing; because those are their functional things, the fuel <term>upadana</term> <gloss>appropriated material</gloss> and that which arises from the fuel—the light and the lamp—exist in the relationship of support and supported. As for how that occurs, the fact that this change itself is the faultless characteristic of appropriation was already shown previously. Again, it is repeated.

<summary>This page analyzes the logical relationship between a support and its perishing, arguing that consciousness acts as the primary linker between objects. It distinguishes between ultimate meeting and conceptual designation using the metaphor of a lamp and its fuel.</summary>
<keywords>refutation, support, perishing, mental consciousness, conceptual thought, lamp metaphor, appropriation</keywords>

is clearly shown; this means it is explicitly stated. The explanation follows: *whatever specific transformation*, and so on. Regarding the phrase *from what cause*, it refers to the cause that makes it known, and this relates to the observation. Regardless of which term one considers, the conclusion is drawn from that very cause; one should connect this by saying that at that time, causes such as hatred are also observed to be present. Alternatively, the phrase *from what cause* connects to what preceded it; it should be applied to the question of *which specific transformation* occurs in relation to which of the humors <term>doshas</term> <gloss>bodily constituents in Ayurvedic medicine</gloss>, such as wind <term>vayu</term>, which are the causes of desire and the rest. Regarding the phrase *at that time*, one should place *that cause* first in relation to whatever term is used, and apply it to the *nature of all things*. 

Because desire and the other afflictions are not definitely fixed to specific humors like bile <term>pitta</term>, they do not constitute the nature of everything. Furthermore, the specific states residing in bile and the other humors would become the nature of every variety of desire and so forth. This is because the error is the same. It is because of that cause, which clearly shows that desire and the rest are identical in nature. If one wonders why this is incorrect, the text says *that too*, referring to the specific transformation of phlegm <term>kapha</term> and the others. Even if any specific variation of wind and the other humors were the cause, not every variation would be endowed with every instance of desire and the rest. This should be inferred because we see a definite result at all times. 

The objection is raised: *However, if the result...* because it possesses the cooperation of a definite distinction. Well then, that specific cooperating cause which is definite is nothing other than habituation <term>vasana</term> <gloss>mental impressions or tendencies</gloss>; for we see the distinctions of desire and so forth arising from the distinctions of that habituation. The reply to the idea that if one posits another cause, even smoke would not be established as having fire as its cause, is the phrase: *What smoke is seen without fire?* Since smoke is possessed of fire, fire exists in that place. If one then thinks that fire itself is the cause of the smoke but the location is not, the text says: *It is not so*, thus raising a doubt.

<summary>This page continues a logical debate regarding whether bodily humors like wind, bile, and phlegm can be the primary causes of mental afflictions like desire and hatred. The author argues that mental habits and tendencies are the true causes, using the analogy of smoke and fire to discuss causal relationships.</summary>
<keywords>humors, doshas, desire, hatred, phlegm, bile, wind, causality, habituation, vasana, logic, Pramanavarttika</keywords>

With regard to the statement starting with **what is the nature of cessation** <note>original: "chad ngo bo gang yin pas"</note>, there are two types of destruction: the nature of the cessation of a continuum, and the characteristic of giving rise to a dissimilar continuum. Regarding these, if one speaks by taking destruction to be the nature of the cessation of a continuum, that is incorrect. With regard to the statement **it does not exist in the end either** <note>original: "de ni mthar yang yod pa ma yin"</note>, because it lacks an essence, why state **how could it exist even in the end?** <note>original: "de ni mthar yang ji ltar 'gyur"</note>. Therefore, since this is never accepted as existing at any time, the consequence that the thing does not exist at the beginning or the end is simply irrelevant. 

Similarly, this is merely a refutation of the production that arises through the connection of another moment of the same type of duration. When it is explained in relation to a vase and so forth, the meaning is that "that very thing does not arise," but it is not a positive proof of anything. Furthermore, if one asserts the second kind of destruction characterized by the production of a dissimilar moment, it is not established as being causeless, because it is explicitly accepted that such a thing is produced by the power of causes such as a hammer. For that very reason, this does not arise at the first <note>at the moment of the object's initial formation</note>, because at that time its own cause, the hammer and so forth, is absent.

In order to establish the arrangement of contradictions, the text states **two types of momentary things** <note>original: "skad cig ma yi dngos rnam gnyis"</note> and so forth. Some things act as causes for contraction <note>diminishment</note> through a sequence of producing moments that are slightly weaker, moderately weaker, or much weaker; for example, like fire in relation to cold. Others are not like that and are not causes of decline, such as fire in relation to smoke and the like. Regarding those, although the causes of contraction shown first exist in a cause-and-effect relationship, the world, whose vision of knowledge is obscured by the cataracts of ignorance, mistakenly imagines them to be contradictory. 

The phrase **various types** <note>original: "rnam pa du ma"</note> refers to distinctions such as fire which is the opposite of cold, wind in relation to a lamp, and darkness in relation to light. In the ultimate sense <note>original: "don dam par"</note>, among entities, there is no such thing as an entity that harms or an entity that is harmed. Because an existing thing is established by its entire self, it cannot be transformed into another nature.

<summary>This page discusses two types of destruction: the total cessation of a continuum and the transition to a dissimilar state. It argues that while some changes appear contradictory to the ignorant, they follow a causal sequence where moments are produced by specific conditions like a hammer or fire.</summary>
<keywords>destruction, continuum, causality, contradiction, momentary nature, Buddhist logic, nature of things</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>and so forth, there would be no perception of diversity at all. In paintings and the like, there is no single entity that functions as a whole <note>original: "yan lag can", Sanskrit: "avayavin", the "possessor of parts"</note>. If you ask what it is then, it consists of various qualities such as blue and so forth. It is not correct to understand that the perception is produced by <note>a single whole</note>. In this way, it does not possess diversity. Why? Because it lacks form <note>original: "gzugs med", meaning it lacks substantial visible form as a single unit</note>. The quality of possession, being an attribute itself, does not have another quality called "form," because qualities do not possess other qualities.

If one argues that even though the object of sound is not diverse in nature, it is still described as "diverse" by way of metaphor, because it shares common characteristics with the diverse nature of a whole—such as is found in a variegated butterfly—we reply: a mere metaphor cannot be the basis <note>of the perception</note>. Which possesses the pure radiance of those who perform merit,
Whose nature is like the Ganges in its strength of heart,
It remains within a stainless mind.
At one time, possessing the flowers of fame,
With the fragrance of merit fully expanded,
In the joy-bestowing garden of good deeds,
In that city...
